newsitem.title: INDIA: India Congress says open for talks to end crisis.
newsitem.headline: India Congress says open for talks to end crisis.

text.p: India's Congress party said on Friday it was open for talks with the ruling coalition to end a political crisis the party started just days ago by withdrawing crucial support from the government.
Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters the party stood behind party president Sitaram Kesri, but added that talks with Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left alliance were possible.
In response to a question whether Congress was ready for talks to end the crisis, Gadgil said: "Let the proposal come." Asked if the Congress was open for talks, he said: "Yes, yes."

Politicians said hectic talks were taking place behind the scenes between middle-ranking Congress leaders and willing counterparts in the United Front to make peace and avoid premature elections after the last polls held a year ago.
The party was not scheduled to hold any meetings of senior leaders and Kesri was in charge, Gadgil said. "The party is one. There is no need to announce it," he said.

Kesri withdrew the party's make-or-break support to the minority government headed by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Sunday, citing economic drift and the government's weakness in containing Hindu nationalists in the opposition.
The 15-party coalition, made up of centrists, regional groups and communists is scheduled to face a vote of confidence in the lower house of parliament on April 11.
Analysts said there was every sign the Congress Party was faltering in its claim to lead an alternative coalition, and Deve Gowda was receiving firm support from coalition partners.

Deve Gowda can survive against the Congress only if the main opposition Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) lawmakers abstain wholly or partially in the vote of confidence, in which the government needs a simple majority of members present and voting.
The BJP and its allies control 193 votes in the 545-seat lower house. The United Front has 180 votes and Congress 140.
On Thursday, the United Front snubbed a key demand from the Congress to replace Deve Gowda after Kesri said on Tuesday that the Congress would reconsider its position if he resigned.
The alliance also ruled out supporting a Congress bid for power.
"What is significant is that the Congress in the past few days has come to terms with reality," said analyst Mahesh Rangarajan of New Delhi's Centre for Contemporary Studies.

He said the Congress, which had in 1980 and 1990 had successfully inspired splits and defections in the then ruling anti-Congress coalitions, no longer appeared to be a strong magnet that could draw smaller groups.

Deve Gowda is seen by analysts as having assumed the free-market reform agenda that the Congress initiated in 1991, and backing it up with a accommodative style that pleases regional coalition partners.
"I really think that they (regional groups) have a stake in a loosely federal system," Rangarajan said. "For the first time, we have had cooperative federalism," he said.

Deve Gowda's Finance Minister, P. Chidambaram, presented on February 28 a market-friendly budget for 1997/98 (April-March) that industry is keen to get approved. The United Front says the budget is linked to its own future.
The coalition has said the Congress Party would accept a face-saving formula to avoid elections.
"Congressmen think Kesri is heading them towards a snap poll, and a snap poll is the last thing the Congress party can afford," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said on Thursday.
A recent opinion poll said the BJP would gain at the Congress's expense if there were mid-term elections.
